questions.q: . If $A+B+C=\pi$, then $\left|\begin{array}{ccc}\sin (A+B+C) & \sin B & \cos C \\ -\sin B & 0 & \tan A \\ \cos (A+B) & -\tan A & 0\end{array}\right|$ is equal to
questions.solution:
In a triangle $A B C$, $A+B+C=\pi$, $\Rightarrow \sin (A+B+C)=0, \cos (A+B)=-\cos C\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad\left|\begin{array}{ccc}\sin (A+B+C) & \sin B & \cos C \\ -\sin B & 0 & \tan A \\ \cos (A+B) & -\tan A & 0\end{array}\right| \\ \quad=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}0 & \sin B & \cos C \\ -\sin B & 0 & \tan A \\ -\cos C & -\tan A & 0\end{array}\right|\end{aligned}$
=0 $\therefore \text{It is the determinant of a skew symmetric matrix of odd order. }$

options: scalar but not an identity matrix

questions.q: Let $D=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}n & n^2 & n^3 \\ n^2 & n^3 & n^5 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{array}\right|$, then $\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{M_{11}+C_{33}}{\left(M_{13}\right)^2}$ is equal to (where $M_{i j}$ is the minor and $C_{i j}$ is the cofactor of $i^{\text {th }}$ row and $j^{\text {th }}$ column's element)
questions.solution:
$\because D=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
n & n^2 & n^3 \\
n^2 & n^3 & n^5 \\
1 & 2 & 3
\end{array}\right|$
Then, $M_{11}=\left|\begin{array}{cc}n^3 & n^5 \\ 2 & 3\end{array}\right|=3 n^3-2 n^5$
and $C_{33}=\left|\begin{array}{cc}n & n^2 \\ n^2 & n^3\end{array}\right|=n^4-n^4=0\begin{aligned}
M_{13} & =\left|\begin{array}{cc}
n^2 & n^3 \\
1 & 2
\end{array}\right|=2 n^2-n^3 \\
\therefore  \lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} & =\frac{M_{11}+C_{33}}{\left(M_{13}\right)^2}=\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{n^3\left(3-2 n^2\right)+0}{n^4(2-n)^2} \\
& =\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{3-2 n^2}{n\left[4+n^2-4 n\right]}=\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{n^2\left(\frac{3}{n^2}-2\right)}{n^3\left(\frac{4}{n^2}+1-\frac{4}{n}\right)}
\end{aligned}$
put $n=\infty=\frac{\left(\frac{3}{\infty^2}-2\right)}{\infty\left(\frac{4}{\infty^2}+1-\frac{4}{\infty}\right)}=\frac{-2}{1 \times \infty}=0$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $P=\left[\begin{array}{cc}\sqrt{3} / 2 & 1 / 2 \\ -1 / 2 & \sqrt{3} / 2\end{array}\right], A=\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{array}\right]$ and $Q=P A P^{\prime}$, then $P^{\prime} Q^{2005} P$ is
questions.solution:
We have,
$P^{\prime} P=\left[\begin{array}{cc}\sqrt{3} / 2 & 1 / 2 \\ -1 / 2 & \sqrt{3} / 2\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{cc}\sqrt{3} / 2 & -1 / 2 \\ 1 / 2 & \sqrt{3} / 2\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{ll}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{array}\right]\begin{array}{lrl}\Rightarrow & P^{\prime} P & =I \text { or } P^{\prime}=P^{-1} \\ \text { As, } & Q & =P A P^{\prime}\end{array}
$\therefore P^{\prime} Q^{2005} P=P^{\prime}\left[\left(P A P^{\prime}\right)\left(P A P^{\prime}\right) \ldots 2005\right.$ times $] P=\underbrace{\left(P^{\prime} P\right) A\left(P^{\prime} P\right) A\left(P^{\prime} P\right) \ldots\left(P^{\prime} P\right) A\left(P^{\prime} P\right)}_{2005 \text { times }}=I A^{2005}=A^{2005}$
Now, $\quad A=\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{array}\right]^{\prime} A^2=\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{array}\right]A^3=\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1\end{array}\right] \ldots A^{2005}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1 & 2005 \\ 0 & 1\end{array}\right]\therefore P^{\prime} Q^{2005} P=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1 & 2005 \\ 0 & 1\end{array}\right]

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $A$ is a square matrix such that $A^2=A$ and $(1+A)^n=I+\lambda A$, then $\lambda$ is equal to
questions.solution:
We have,
$A^2=A\therefore(I+A)^2=(I+A)(I+A)=I+2 A+A^2=I+3 A$
and
$(I+A)^3=(I+A)^2(I+A)\begin{array}{lr}=(I+3 A)(I+A) & {\left[\because(I+A)^2=I+3 A\right]} \\ =I+4 A+3 A^2 & \\ =I+7 A & {\left[\because A^2=A\right]}\end{array}
Thus, we have
$(I+A)^2=I+3 A$ and $(I+A)^3=I+7 A\Rightarrow \quad(I+A)^2=I+\left(2^2-1\right) A$
and $\quad(I+A)^3=I+\left(2^3-1\right) A$
Hence, $(I+A)^n=I+\left(2^n-1\right) A\begin{aligned} \therefore & & (I+A)^n & =I+\lambda A \\ \Rightarrow & & \lambda & =2^n-1\end{aligned}

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $A$ and $n \times n$ non-singular matrix such that $A A^T=A^{-1} A$ and $B=A^{-1} A^T$, then $B B^{\prime}$ is equal to
questions.solution:
If $A$ is non-singular matrix, then $|A| \neq 0\begin{aligned}
A A^T & =A^{-1} A \text { and } B=A^{-1} A^T \\
\Rightarrow \quad B B^{\prime} & =\left(A^{-1} A^T\right)\left(A^{-1} A^T\right)^T \\
& =A^{-1} A^T \cdot A\left(A^{-1}\right)^T \quad\left[\because(A I)^{\prime}=A\right] \\
& =A^{-1} A A^T\left(A^{-1}\right)^T \\
& =I A^T\left(A^{-1}\right)^T \\
& =A^T\left(A^{-1}\right)^T \\
& =\left(A^{-1} A\right)^T \quad\left[\because(A B)^T=B^T A^T\right] \\
& =I^T=1
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $a \neq \pm b$ and $\left[\begin{array}{ccc}a & a^2 & 1+a^3 \\ b & b^2 & 1+b^3 \\ 1 & 1 & 2\end{array}\right]=0$, then $a b$ is equal to
questions.solution: Given that, $\left|\begin{array}{ccc}a & a^2 & 1+a^3 \\ b & b^2 & 1+b^3 \\ 1 & 1 & 1+1\end{array}\right|=0\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow\left|\begin{array}{lll}a & a^2 & 1 \\ b & b^2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right|+\left|\begin{array}{ccc}a & a^2 & a^3 \\ b & b^2 & b^3 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right|=0 \\ & \Rightarrow\left|\begin{array}{ccc}a & a^2 & 1 \\ b & b^2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right|+a b\left|\begin{array}{ccc}1 & a & a^2 \\ 1 & b & b^2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right|=0 \\ & \Rightarrow(a b+1)\left|\begin{array}{ccc}a & a^2 & 1 \\ b & b^2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right|=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad(a b+1)\left[a\left(b^2-1\right)-a^2(b-1)+1\left(b-b^2\right)\right]=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad(a b+1)(b-1)[a(b+1)-a-b)]=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad(a b+1)(b-1)[a b+a-a-b]=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad b(a b+1)(b-1)(a-1)=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad b=0,1; a=1, ab=-1 \end{aligned}$

questions.q:
Let $A=\left[\begin{array}{ll}0 & \alpha \\ 0 & 0\end{array}\right]$ and $(A+I)^{50}-50 A=\left[\begin{array}{ll}a & b \\ c & d\end{array}\right]$,
then the value of $a+b+c+d$ is
questions.solution:
As. $A^2=0, A^K=0 \quad \forall K \geq 2$
Thus, $\quad(A+I)^{50}=I+50 A\Rightarrow \quad(A+I)^{50}-50 A=I\therefore \quad I=\left[\begin{array}{ll}a & b \\ c & d\end{array}\right]\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow a=1, b=0, c=0, d=1 \\ & \therefore \quad a+b+c+d=1+0+0+1=2\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Let $A$ be a square matrix all of whose entries are integers. Then, which one of the following is true?
options: If $\operatorname{det}(A)= \pm 1$, then $A^{-1}$ exists but all its entries are not necessarily integers
If $\operatorname{det}(A) \neq \pm 1$, then $A^{-1}$ exists and all its entries are non-integers

If det (A) $= \pm 1$, then
$A^{-1}$ exists and all its entries are integers
questions.solution:
As $\operatorname{det}(A)= \pm 1, A^{-1}$ exists and
$A^{-1}=\frac{1}{\operatorname{det}(A)}(\operatorname{adj} A)= \pm \operatorname{adj} A$
All entries in adj $(A)$ are integers.
$\therefore A^{-1}$ has integer entries.

questions.q: For two unimodular complex numbers $z_1$ and $z_2,\left[\begin{array}{ll}\bar{z}_1 & z_2 \\ \bar{z}_2 & z_1\end{array}\right]^{-1}\left[\begin{array}{cc}z_1 & z_2 \\ -\bar{z}_2 & \bar{z}_1\end{array}\right]^{-1}$ is equal to
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & {\left[\begin{array}{cc}\bar{z}_1 & -z_2 \\ \bar{z}_2 & z_1\end{array}\right]^{-1}\left[\begin{array}{cc}z_1 & z_2 \\ -\bar{z}_2 & \bar{z}_1\end{array}\right]^{-1} } \\ &=\left\{\left[\begin{array}{cc}z_1 & z_2 \\ -\bar{z}_2 & \bar{z}_1\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{cc}\bar{z}_1 & -z_2 \\ \bar{z}_2 & z_1\end{array}\right]\right\}^{-1} \\ &=\left[\begin{array}{cc}z_1 \bar{z}_1+z_2 \bar{z}_2 & 0 \\ 0 & z_2 \bar{z}_2+z_1 \bar{z}_1\end{array}\right]^{-1} \\ &=\left[\begin{array}{cc}\left|z_1\right|^2+\left|z_2\right|^2 & 0 \\ 0 & \left|z_1\right|^2+\left|z_2\right|^2\end{array}\right]^{-1} \\ &=\left[\begin{array}{cc}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{array}\right]^{-1}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1 / 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 / 2\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $A$ is a square matrix of order $n$ such that $|\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj} A)|=|A|^9$, then the value of $n$ can be
questions.solution: We know that, in a square matrix of order $n|\operatorname{adj} A|=|A|^{n-1}\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow|\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj} A)|=|\operatorname{adj} A|^{n-1}=|A|^{(n-1)^2} \\ & \Rightarrow n^2-2 n-8=0 \\ & \Rightarrow n=4 \text { as } n=-2 \text { is not possible. }\end{aligned}$

questions.q: Let $A=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & -3 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right]$ and $10 B=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}4 & 2 & 2 \\ -5 & 0 & \alpha \\ 1 & -2 & 3\end{array}\right]$. If $B$ is the inverse of matrix $A$, then $\alpha$ is
questions.solution: Given, $\left[\begin{array}{ccc}4 & 2 & 2 \\ -5 & 0 & \alpha \\ 1 & -2 & 3\end{array}\right]=10 A^{-1}\therefore \quad\left[\begin{array}{ccc}4 & 2 & 2 \\ -5 & 0 & \alpha \\ 1 & -2 & 3\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & -3 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right]\begin{aligned} & ={\left[\begin{array}{ccc}10 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 10 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 10\end{array}\right] } \\ \Rightarrow \quad & {\left[\begin{array}{ccc}10 & 0 & 0 \\ -5+\alpha & 5+\alpha & -5+\alpha \\ 0 & 0 & 10\end{array}\right] } \\ & =\left[\begin{array}{ccc}10 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 10 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 10\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}\begin{array}{ll}\Rightarrow & -5+\alpha=0 \\ \Rightarrow & \alpha=5\end{array}$
